title: Dimorphic Fungi: Mold in the Cold, Yeast in the Heat
summary: Follow a spore from warm soil to the lung, learn which fungi switch from mold to yeast with temperature, and recognize Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides spherules in tissue — while respecting the infectious mold in the lab.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 60 Hit 1 (core: thermal dimorphism), Hit 2 (Histoplasma vs Blastomyces tissue forms), Hit 3 (Coccidioides spherules, arthroconidia, BSL-3) and the Figure 60 memory anchor. Checked against Gauthier 2015, Poplin 2021, Shah 2017 and Crum 2022. Pending: Histoplasma size (3–5 µm) and narrow-based budding, and the reviewer’s “do not convert Coccidioides in the lab”.

objectives: Define thermal dimorphism and list the main thermally dimorphic fungi.
Recognize the tissue forms of Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides.
Explain why mold cultures, especially Coccidioides, require biosafety precautions.

scenes.title: Mold in the soil, yeast in the lung
scenes.altText: A dusty soil scene with fluffy mold threads and floating spores. A spore is inhaled; inside the warm lung the same organism appears as round yeast cells. A thermometer token shifts from about 25 °C to 37 °C.

cues.text: In the soil, some fungi grow as fluffy mold, shedding spores into the air.
Breathe those spores in, and in the warmth of the lung the very same fungus turns into yeast.
That switch with temperature is called thermal dimorphism, and it is the key to a group of important fungal infections.

scenes.title: Normal: who is thermally dimorphic
scenes.altText: A two-column chart: environment / culture at room temperature (about 22–25 °C) = mold producing infectious conidia; body (37 °C) = yeast, except Coccidioides, which forms spherules. Members listed: Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Sporothrix, Talaromyces (formerly Penicillium) marneffei, Emmonsia. Temperature is the main trigger; CO₂ and other factors also influence the switch.

cues.text: Thermally dimorphic fungi grow as mold at environmental temperatures — about 22 to 25 degrees — producing infectious spores called conidia.
At body temperature, 37 degrees, they convert to yeast. Coccidioides is the exception: it forms spherules instead.
The group includes Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Sporothrix and Talaromyces marneffei, formerly called Penicillium marneffei.
Temperature is the main trigger, though carbon dioxide and other factors also influence the switch.

scenes.title: What changes: three tissue forms to recognize
scenes.altText: Three magnified tissue panels. Histoplasma: small oval budding yeasts, often inside macrophages (histiocytes). Blastomyces: larger yeasts, about 8–15 µm, with a thick double-contoured wall and broad-based budding. Coccidioides: large thick-walled spherules (sources give about 10–200 µm) packed with 2–5 µm endospores, which are released when the spherule ruptures. Beside Coccidioides, the culture form: barrel-shaped arthroconidia (3–5 µm) alternating with empty cells.

cues.text: Histoplasma in tissue is a small, oval, budding yeast, often packed inside macrophages.
Blastomyces is larger — about 8 to 15 micrometres — with a thick, double-contoured wall and a characteristic broad-based bud.
Coccidioides doesn’t bud at all. It forms big, thick-walled spherules filled with endospores of about 2 to 5 micrometres. When a spherule bursts, the endospores spread and form new spherules.
In culture, Coccidioides grows as a mold whose hyphae break into barrel-shaped arthroconidia — the highly infectious form.

props.label: Culture: barrel-shaped arthroconidia (3–5 µm) — highly infectious

scenes.title: In the lab: safety and diagnosis
scenes.altText: A biosafety cabinet with a culture plate taped shut. Tokens: tell the laboratory when coccidioidomycosis is suspected; tape plates; work with the mold in a biosafety level 3 cabinet. A diagnosis card lists the tools for endemic fungi: culture, histopathology (spherules, broad-based budding yeast), antigen tests and antibody tests, often in combination.

cues.text: The mold form is the dangerous one in the lab, because it releases infectious spores. Coccidioides arthroconidia are notorious for laboratory infections.
So if coccidioidomycosis is suspected, tell the laboratory, tape the plates shut, and handle the mold in a biosafety level 3 cabinet.
Diagnosis often needs several tools: culture, histopathology showing spherules or broad-based budding yeast, and antigen and antibody tests.
Seeing spherules in tissue, or growing Coccidioides in culture, is the diagnostic standard for coccidioidomycosis.

props.label: Cocci standard: spherules in tissue or positive culture

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “A budding yeast in tissue = Coccidioides” is crossed out → “Coccidioides forms spherules with endospores; it does not bud. Two endospores side by side can mimic budding.” Trap card: “The yeast form is what infects lab workers” is crossed out → “The mold (spores) is infectious; Coccidioides cultures need BSL-3 precautions.”

cues.text: Trap one: Coccidioides doesn’t bud. It forms spherules full of endospores. Two endospores lying side by side can look like a bud — don’t be fooled.
Trap two: in the lab, the danger is the mold form with its spores, not the tissue yeast. Coccidioides cultures need biosafety level 3 precautions.
And remember the size ladder: small Histoplasma inside macrophages, larger thick-walled Blastomyces with a broad bud, giant spherules for Coccidioides.

scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Mold in the cold, yeast in the heat.” Then the size ladder as three cartoon stepping stones: Histo small and hiding in macrophages, Blasto big with a Broad Bud, Cocci a giant bag of endospores. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: mold in the cold, yeast in the heat. Then climb the ladder: Histo is small and hides in macrophages; Blasto is big, with a broad bud; Cocci is a giant bag of endospores.

Where it breaks: Coccidioides makes spherules, not yeast; Sporothrix and others have their own tissue forms; sizes overlap and vary between sources; and conversion in the lab is not always tried — some molds are identified by other methods.

explanation.what: Plain language: some fungi change shape with temperature — fluffy mold in the soil, yeast in the body. Scientific terms: thermally dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Sporothrix, Talaromyces marneffei, Emmonsia) grow as mycelia producing conidia at ~22–25 °C and convert to yeast (Coccidioides: spherules) at 37 °C.
explanation.why: Inhaled conidia or hyphal fragments convert in the warm host; temperature is the major stimulus, with CO₂ and other factors contributing. Tissue forms differ: Histoplasma small oval budding yeasts often within histiocytes; Blastomyces 8–15 µm yeasts with thick double-contoured walls and broad-based budding; Coccidioides thick-walled spherules (≈10–200 µm, depending on source) with 2–5 µm endospores, and barrel-shaped 3–5 µm arthroconidia in culture.
explanation.measure: Culture, histopathology, antigen and antibody tests, often combined; for coccidioidomycosis, spherules in tissue or culture are the standard. Inform the lab, tape plates and work in a BSL-3 cabinet when Coccidioides is suspected.
explanation.differs: Mold (environment/culture, infectious) vs yeast/spherule (tissue); budding yeasts (Histoplasma, Blastomyces) vs non-budding spherules (Coccidioides).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: definition and members of the dimorphic group, tissue-form identification by size and budding, spherule vs yeast, and lab safety for Coccidioides.

comparisons.title: Coccidioides: tissue vs culture
comparisons.distinguisher: Temperature and setting decide the form — and the hazard.

mnemonic.text: Mold in the cold, yeast in the heat.
mnemonic.explanation: Thermally dimorphic fungi are molds at environmental temperature and yeasts at 37 °C; then the size ladder — small Histo in macrophages, big broad-budding Blasto, giant Cocci spherules.
mnemonic.limitation: Coccidioides forms spherules rather than yeast; other dimorphs have distinct tissue forms; sizes overlap and vary by source; identification does not always require conversion.

analogyLimitations: Drawn yeasts, spherules and spores are schematic and not to scale.
The soil-to-lung story simplifies exposure routes (e.g. Sporothrix enters through skin).
takeaway: Thermally dimorphic fungi grow as infectious mold in the cool environment and as yeast — or, for Coccidioides, spherules — at body temperature, so recognize the tissue form and treat the mold culture as the hazard.

questions.stem: A lung biopsy shows large thick-walled structures filled with small round endospores, with no budding. Which organism is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. Spherules containing endospores are the tissue form of Coccidioides.
Incorrect. Blastomyces shows thick-walled yeasts with broad-based budding.
Incorrect. Histoplasma shows small budding yeasts, often inside macrophages.
Incorrect. Candida forms yeasts and pseudohyphae, not spherules.

questions.stem: Yeasts about 8–15 µm with thick, double-contoured walls and broad-based buds are seen in sputum. What is the most likely organism?

options.rationale: Correct. Size, thick wall and broad-based budding are characteristic.
Incorrect. Histoplasma yeasts are smaller and often intracellular.
Incorrect. Coccidioides forms spherules, not budding yeasts.
Incorrect. Aspergillus forms septate hyphae, not yeasts.

questions.stem: A culture plate from a patient with suspected coccidioidomycosis is growing a white mold. What is the most important precaution?

options.text: Keep the plate taped and handle it only in a biosafety level 3 cabinet
options.rationale: Correct. The mold releases highly infectious arthroconidia.

options.text: Open the plate on the bench to examine the colony
options.rationale: Incorrect. Opening a Coccidioides mold culture on the bench risks inhaling arthroconidia.

options.text: Incubate at 37 °C so the tissue yeast form becomes infectious
options.rationale: Incorrect. The mold form, not the tissue form, is the laboratory hazard.

options.text: No special precautions are needed for fungi
options.rationale: Incorrect. Coccidioides cultures need BSL-3 precautions.

claims.text: Thermally dimorphic fungi: mold with conidia at ~22–25 °C, yeast (Coccidioides: spherules) at 37 °C; members listed; temperature main trigger.

Histoplasma small oval budding yeast in histiocytes; Blastomyces 8–15 µm thick double-contoured wall, broad-based budding; Coccidioides spherules (10–200 µm) with 2–5 µm endospores, adjacent endospores mimic budding.
Coccidioides culture: barrel-shaped 3–5 µm arthroconidia; inform lab, tape plates, BSL-3 cabinet; spherules or culture as diagnostic standard.
Histoplasma yeasts are 3–5 µm with narrow-based budding.
claims.note: Sources read describe “small oval budding yeast” without size or bud width.

claims.text: Coccidioides is not routinely converted from mold to yeast in the lab; screw-capped slants used.
claims.note: Not taught; not stated in the sources read.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives Coccidioides spherules “up to 100 µm”; sources read give 20–100 µm and 10–200 µm. The lesson notes that sizes vary by source.
